questions.explanation: The back button pops with no value, so the future completes with null. That is why the result type is `bool?` and why you always have to handle the null — the user closing the screen without choosing is a normal outcome, not an error.
whyWrong: `false` would mean the screen had explicitly popped `false`. It popped nothing.
`true` would require an explicit choice, and there was none.
Nothing throws: a pop with no value is completely normal.

questions.prompt: In go_router, what is the difference between `context.go` and `context.push`?
options: `go` sets the stack from the URL, `push` adds one on top
questions.explanation: `go` is the declarative one: the path says what the stack should be, and the framework builds it. `push` is the old behaviour, adding one screen on top. Use `go` for a deep link or a tab, and `push` for drilling into a detail.
whyWrong: They behave quite differently, and picking the wrong one gives you a back button that goes somewhere unexpected.
Both work everywhere. The web only makes the difference more visible.
Neither waits for anything in that sense.

questions.prompt: With `GoRoute(path: '/users/:id')`, how do you read `42` from `/users/42`?
questions.explanation: A `:name` in the path becomes an entry in `pathParameters`. That is the whole point of declaring routes as paths: the parameter is extracted for you, with no parsing by hand.
whyWrong: `extra` is for passing an object that is not in the URL, and it does not survive a deep link.
Query parameters are what comes after a `?`. The 42 here is part of the path.
That is the Navigator 1.0 way of reading untyped arguments.

questions.prompt: Why was the Router API (Navigator 2.0) introduced?
options: To describe the stack declaratively: web URLs and deep links
questions.explanation: A stack built by a series of pushes cannot be rebuilt from a URL, which is what the browser's address bar and forward button require. The Router API turns it round: you describe the whole stack for a given state, and the framework works out the difference.
whyWrong: Hero animations worked perfectly well with Navigator 1.0.
`MaterialPageRoute` is still there and still used by go_router.
It could pop fine. The problem was describing a stack from the outside.

questions.prompt: Where do you put "if not logged in, go to /login" with go_router?
questions.explanation: `redirect` runs before every navigation, so the rule lives in one place and covers deep links and restored sessions as well. Checking in each screen means repeating yourself and forgetting one.
whyWrong: Repeated in every screen, and the one you forget is the hole.
Before `runApp` you only know the state at startup, not at every navigation.
`onGenerateRoute` belongs to Navigator 1.0 and is not used by go_router.

questions.prompt: A bottom bar where each tab keeps its own history:
options: StatefulShellRoute, or one Navigator per tab
questions.explanation: Each tab needs its own stack, so that going deep in one and switching away and back returns you to where you were. `StatefulShellRoute` gives each branch its own navigator and keeps its state.
whyWrong: A single stack means switching tabs throws away where you were in the previous one.
An `IndexedStack` keeps the widgets alive but gives no per-tab navigation history.
Named routes do not create separate stacks.

questions.prompt: What is the main limitation of named routes?
options: Limited deep links, and the browser's forward button does not work
They do not work on iOS
questions.explanation: A stack built by pushes cannot be reconstructed from a URL, so the browser cannot go forward and a path with a parameter has to be parsed by hand. That is exactly the gap the Router API, and go_router on top of it, were made to fill.
whyWrong: They do take arguments — just untyped ones you have to cast.
They are still there and still work for simple apps.
They work on every platform. It is the web where the limits show.

questions.prompt: What do you need on iOS to open the app from an https link?
options: Associated Domains, and the apple-app-site-association file on the site
questions.explanation: The system fetches that file from your site and checks that the site really does vouch for your app. That verification is what stops another app claiming your links, and it is why an https link is safer than a custom scheme.
whyWrong: No channel is involved: the system delivers the link to the app.
The manifest is Android's half. iOS needs its own configuration.
It does not: without the file and the entitlement, the link opens the website instead.

topics.title: Isolates: doing heavy work elsewhere
topics.summary: Dart has no threads sharing memory. What it has instead, why that removes a whole class of bug, and when it is worth the trouble.

lesson.heading: No shared memory, by design
lesson.body:
In most languages, concurrency means threads sharing memory — and with that come the two hardest bugs there are: **races**, where two threads touch the same value at once and the result is nonsense, and **deadlocks**, where two threads wait for each other forever.

Dart made a different choice. An **isolate** is a line of execution with its **own memory and its own event loop**. Nothing is shared. Two isolates cannot touch the same object, because neither can see the other's objects at all.

So there are no locks, because there is nothing to lock. And races and deadlocks are not avoided by being careful — they are **impossible**.

The price is communication: isolates talk by **sending messages**, and a message is **copied**. You cannot hand an object across; a copy arrives at the other end. For small results that is nothing; for very large ones the copy is itself a cost worth knowing about.

The second thing to be clear about: your app's interface runs on one isolate, the **root isolate**, and it is the only one allowed to touch widgets. Everything else is a helper.

lesson.heading: When it is worth it, and when it is not
lesson.body:
This is the question that actually gets asked, and the answer is one distinction: **waiting is not working**.

**Waiting** is a network call, reading a file, a query. The processor is doing nothing; it is just not finished. `async`/`await` already handles this perfectly: the function suspends, the thread goes off and draws frames, and it resumes when the answer arrives. **An isolate here adds cost and gains nothing.**

**Working** is calculation: parsing ten megabytes of JSON, resizing an image, encrypting, sorting a huge list. Here the processor is genuinely busy, nothing suspends, and no amount of `async` helps. Dart runs on one thread per isolate, so for the whole second your interface is frozen.

Sixteen milliseconds is the budget for a frame. Anything over that is a dropped frame; a few hundred milliseconds is a visible stutter; a second is an app that looks broken.

So the rule: **an isolate for calculation that takes longer than a frame. Never for input and output.**

And a thing worth knowing before reaching for one: often the real answer is not to do the work at all. Asking the server for less data, or parsing it as it streams in, beats parsing it faster.

lesson.heading: Isolate.run and compute
lesson.body:
You rarely need to create an isolate by hand. Two helpers cover nearly everything.

**`Isolate.run`** — in the Dart standard library. Give it a function, and it starts an isolate, runs it, hands back the result and shuts the isolate down. One line, and the lifetime is managed for you.

**`compute`** — Flutter's older equivalent, which takes a function and one argument. It is still everywhere in existing code and still works; `Isolate.run` is simply more flexible.

The constraint that catches people, and it follows directly from unshared memory: the function you pass **cannot capture things from around it in the usual way**. With `compute` it has to be a **top-level or static function**, because what gets sent across is effectively a reference to a named function, not a closure carrying a captured environment.

`Isolate.run` is more relaxed about this, but the same principle applies: everything the function needs has to be sendable, and anything it captures is copied across. A closure that captures a widget, a `BuildContext` or an open connection cannot be sent, and the error says so.

And starting an isolate is not free — a few milliseconds. For work measured in microseconds, that is worse than doing it inline. For a second of parsing, it is irrelevant.

lesson.heading: Ports: talking to an isolate that stays alive
lesson.body:
`Isolate.run` is right for one piece of work. When you need an isolate that stays alive and handles many requests — a parser you feed continuously, a long calculation reporting progress — you create it yourself with `Isolate.spawn` and talk over **ports**.

A **`ReceivePort`** is where you receive messages. Every receive port has a **`SendPort`**, and that is the thing you can send to another isolate so it knows how to reply. The pattern is always the same: the parent creates a receive port, sends its send port to the child in the first message, and the child replies through it.

Two things to remember:

**Close the ports.** A receive port that is never closed keeps the isolate alive, and you have leaked something much bigger than an object.

**Kill the isolate when you are done**, or it keeps its memory. `Isolate.run` does both for you, which is why it is the default choice.

There is also a trick worth knowing for a very large result: **`Isolate.exit(port, result)`** ends the isolate and hands over the value **without copying it** — since the child is ending, its memory can simply be transferred. For a result of tens of megabytes, that is the difference between fast and noticeably slow.

lesson.heading: The limits: plugins, and the background
lesson.body:
Two limits come up in real apps, and both surprise people the first time.

**Platform channels belong to the root isolate.** A Flutter plugin — `path_provider`, `shared_preferences`, anything that calls native code — talks over a channel that is wired to the root isolate. Call it from another isolate and you get an error about bindings not being initialised.

The fix exists: pass a `RootIsolateToken` to the child and call `BackgroundIsolateBinaryMessenger.ensureInitialized` before touching any plugin. But it is worth asking first whether the plugin call really has to be in there. Usually the clean shape is: read with the plugin on the root isolate, send the data across, do the calculation, send the result back.

**An isolate does not survive the app being suspended.** It is not a separate process: it belongs to your app. When the user leaves and the system suspends the app, every isolate stops with it. On iOS especially, you get a few seconds and no more.

So for work that genuinely has to continue — an upload, a sync — an isolate is the wrong tool. You need the platform's own mechanism: WorkManager on Android, BGTaskScheduler on iOS, or a package that wraps both.

questions.prompt: Why does Dart need no locks between isolates?
options: Because the runtime locks every object implicitly
Because isolates take turns and never run at once
Because each has its own memory and they only talk by messages
Because only the main isolate may write
questions.explanation: Nothing is shared, so there is nothing two isolates could touch at the same time. That makes races and deadlocks impossible rather than merely avoidable — the price being that messages are copied instead of passed.
whyWrong: There is no implicit locking, and it would cost a great deal.
They really can run at the same time, on different cores. It is the lack of sharing that makes it safe.
Every isolate writes freely — to its own memory, which nobody else can see.

questions.prompt: What does `compute(fn, arg)` do?
options: Runs `fn` in a separate isolate and gives back the result
Queues `fn` on the main isolate's event loop
questions.explanation: It starts an isolate, runs the function there, sends the result back and shuts the isolate down. That is why it is the one-line answer for heavy parsing: the calculation happens elsewhere and the interface keeps drawing.
whyWrong: Queueing on the same isolate would still block it when the work finally runs.
It is a Dart isolate, not a native thread. Dart does not expose those.
Nothing is cached: every call does the work again.

questions.prompt: The function is already `async`. Is that enough to avoid the stutter while parsing?
options: Yes: async moves the body to another thread
No: an await is missing before jsonDecode
No: the parsing still runs on the interface isolate
questions.explanation: `async` means the function **can** suspend, not that it runs somewhere else. `jsonDecode` is synchronous and never suspends, so it runs straight through on the same isolate and nothing is drawn for a second. Only an isolate moves the work.
whyWrong: `async` moves nothing: it only allows the function to pause.
`jsonDecode` is synchronous, which is exactly the problem.
You cannot await something that is not asynchronous, and it would change nothing if you could.

questions.prompt: What constraint applies to the function passed to `Isolate.spawn`?
options: It must be top-level or static
It must be in the same file
questions.explanation: The child isolate inherits nothing from the parent, so what is sent across is effectively a reference to a named function. A closure capturing local state would need that state to come too, and it has nowhere to come from.
whyWrong: It can be either. What it must be is reachable by name.
It can return anything: the result is sent back over a port.
The file makes no difference: being top-level or static does.

questions.prompt: How does the child isolate reply to the parent?
options: By returning a value from its entry function
The parent sends it its own SendPort in the first message
questions.explanation: The parent creates a `ReceivePort` and sends its `SendPort` to the child in the initial message. That is the only way the child knows where to reply — there is no shared memory to leave an answer in.
whyWrong: Returning from the entry function tells the parent nothing: nobody is awaiting it.
Globals are not shared: each isolate has its own copy.
There is no such thing: a message always goes to a specific `SendPort`.

questions.prompt: Should you move an HTTP call into an isolate so it does not block the interface?
options: No: input and output are already asynchronous, so the isolate only costs
Yes, or the Future never completes
questions.explanation: A network call is waiting, not working. `await` already suspends the function and frees the thread to draw frames. Adding an isolate means starting one and copying data across, for no benefit at all.
whyWrong: It does not block: the asynchronous API is non-blocking by design.
The behaviour is the same on both platforms.
The future completes perfectly well without any isolate.

questions.prompt: Which of these can you **not** send to another isolate?
options: A closure capturing a local variable
questions.explanation: A closure carries the environment it captured, and that environment lives in the sending isolate's memory, which the other one cannot see. Ports are specifically designed to be sendable, and plain data is copied.
whyWrong: A list of strings is plain data: it is copied across without trouble.
A `SendPort` is made to be sent: it is how the two sides find each other.
A top-level function is sent as a reference by name, which is why `compute` requires one.

questions.prompt: You call a plugin inside a secondary isolate and get a bindings error. Why?
options: Plugins do not work in release builds
Secondary isolates cannot do input or output
Platform channels are tied to the root isolate
questions.explanation: A channel is the bridge to native code, and it is wired to the root isolate. A child isolate has no such bridge until you give it one, by passing a `RootIsolateToken` and calling `BackgroundIsolateBinaryMessenger.ensureInitialized`.
whyWrong: They work in release. The problem is which isolate is calling.
They can read and write files perfectly well. It is the channels that are the issue.
That one is for the root isolate at startup and does not help here.

questions.prompt: How do you return a very large result from an isolate without paying for the copy?
options: A static variable read by the parent
questions.explanation: `Isolate.exit` ends the isolate and hands the value over. Since the child is finishing anyway, its memory can be transferred rather than duplicated. For tens of megabytes that is the difference between instant and noticeably slow.
whyWrong: A normal `send` copies the value, which is exactly the cost you are trying to avoid.
Statics are not shared between isolates: the parent would see nothing.
Killing it destroys the memory. There would be nothing left to hand over.

questions.prompt: Does an isolate keep working when the user leaves the app in the background?
options: Yes on Android, no on iOS
No: when the app is suspended, the isolate stops too
Yes, as long as the ReceivePort stays open
questions.explanation: An isolate belongs to your app's process, so when the system suspends the app everything in it stops — on iOS after a few seconds, on Android when the system decides. Work that must survive needs the platform's own background mechanism, not an isolate.
whyWrong: They are not processes: they are lines of execution inside one.
Both platforms suspend the app, with different timings and rules.
An open port does not keep a suspended app running.

topics.title: Smoothness, native code and tests
topics.summary: Where the sixteen milliseconds go, how to find out instead of guessing, how to call native code, and the three kinds of test.

lesson.heading: Sixteen milliseconds
lesson.body:
A screen refreshes sixty times a second, so each frame has about **16 milliseconds**. On a 120 Hz device it is 8. Take longer and the frame is missed, and a missed frame is a visible stutter — what Flutter people call **jank**.

The work is split between two threads, and knowing which is which is half of diagnosing a problem:

**The UI thread** runs your Dart code: `build`, layout, and working out what to paint. This is where your mistakes usually are.
**The raster thread** turns that into pixels on the GPU. It is slow when there is too much to draw: big shadows, transparency, clipping, filters.

So the first question when something stutters is not "what is slow?" but **"which thread is over budget?"** The performance overlay answers it directly: two graphs, and the one with the red bars is the one to look at.

The three usual causes, in order of how often:

**Too much work in `build`.** Parsing, sorting, formatting — done on every frame.
**Too many rebuilds.** A `setState` high up rebuilding half the screen for a change in one corner.
**Too much repainting.** Shadows and clipping that force the GPU to redo work every frame.

lesson.heading: Rebuilding less, repainting less
lesson.body:
Two separate problems with two separate tools, and confusing them is common.

**Rebuilding** is Dart work. To do less of it:

**`const`** on anything that does not depend on a variable. A `const` widget is literally the same object as last time, so the whole subtree is skipped.
**Push `setState` down.** Put the state in the smallest widget that needs it, so the rebuild is small too.
**The `child` parameter of the animated builders.** This one is worth knowing properly, because it comes up at interview. `AnimatedBuilder` rebuilds its `builder` on every tick of the animation — sixty times a second. Anything expensive in there is rebuilt sixty times a second. Pass it as `child` instead and it is built **once** and handed to the builder, which only wraps it.

**Repainting** is GPU work. The tool is **`RepaintBoundary`**: it puts the subtree on its own layer, so when something next to it repaints, this one is reused rather than redrawn. Right for something expensive and static next to something that animates. Not right everywhere: each boundary costs memory, so scattering them makes things worse.

lesson.heading: Measuring instead of guessing
lesson.body:
Flutter has three build modes, and measuring in the wrong one gives you numbers that mean nothing.

**Debug** — hot reload, assertions, every check switched on. **Several times slower than release.** Never measure here, and never believe a complaint about speed that came from a debug build.
**Profile** — compiled like release but with the measuring tools left in. This is the one to measure in, and **on a real device**: a simulator uses your computer's processor, which is far faster than a phone's.
**Release** — what ships. Fastest, and no tools.

**DevTools** is where the answers are. The Performance view shows each frame and what it spent its time on. The CPU profiler shows which functions. The Memory view finds leaks. And the **rebuild counter** shows which widgets rebuild and how often — usually the quickest way to find the `setState` that is too high up.

And two things about hot reload worth knowing, because the second causes a lot of confusion:

**Hot reload** injects the changed code and **keeps the state**. The widgets rebuild; nothing starts over.
**Hot restart** throws the state away and runs `main()` again.

The consequence: a change to `initState` or to a field's initial value is **not applied by a hot reload**, because that code does not run again. You have to hot restart, and not knowing this costs people an hour at least once.

lesson.heading: Talking to native code
lesson.body:
Flutter draws everything itself, but some things only the platform can do: the battery level, a native sensor, a system dialog, an SDK that only exists for iOS and Android. For those there is a **platform channel**: a bridge between Dart and the native side, over which messages are passed.

Three kinds, and picking the right one is the question:

**`MethodChannel`** — call a native method and get one answer. The usual one.
**`EventChannel`** — receive a **continuous stream** of events from native code: a sensor, the location, the battery changing. It arrives as a `Stream` on the Dart side.
**`BasicMessageChannel`** — messages in both directions with a format you choose. Rare.

The mistake to avoid is polling a `MethodChannel` with a timer to simulate a stream. That is what `EventChannel` is for, and the native side can tell you when something changes rather than being asked sixty times a minute.

Two practical notes. The calls are **asynchronous**, always, because they cross a boundary — so everything is a `Future`. And a failure comes back as a `PlatformException`, which you have to catch: the native side can fail for reasons Dart knows nothing about.

And before writing a channel at all: check pub.dev. The thing you need is very likely already a plugin, written and tested by somebody for both platforms.

lesson.heading: The three kinds of test
lesson.body:
Flutter has three, and they trade speed against realism. A good suite is mostly the first.

**Unit tests** — pure Dart, no widgets, milliseconds each. For business rules, parsing, state holders. This is where most of your tests should be, and if your logic cannot be tested this way it is in the wrong place.

**Widget tests** — build one widget in a fake environment and interact with it. Still fast, hundreds in a few seconds. For "does the right thing appear", "does tapping do what it should".

**Integration tests** — the real app on a real device. Slow, and the only way to test an actual flow end to end, with real plugins and real navigation.

In a widget test the two methods people confuse are **`pump`** and **`pumpAndSettle`**. `pump` advances **one frame**. `pumpAndSettle` keeps advancing until nothing is animating any more. Use `pump` after a change, and `pumpAndSettle` after something that animates — a navigation, a dialog. Using `pumpAndSettle` with an endless animation hangs the test for ever, which is a confusing thing to debug.

There are also **golden tests**: render a widget and compare it with a saved image. They catch visual changes nothing else would, and they fail on a different platform or font version, so they need care.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between hot reload and hot restart?
options: Hot reload keeps the state, hot restart throws it away
Hot restart recompiles the native code
questions.explanation: Hot reload injects the changed code and rebuilds the widgets, keeping where you were and what you had typed. Hot restart starts the app over from `main()`. That is why a change to `initState` needs a restart: that code does not run again on a reload.
whyWrong: They are quite different, and knowing which to use saves a lot of confusion.
Neither recompiles native code: for that you have to stop and run again.
Running `main()` again is what hot restart does.

questions.prompt: Where do you get performance numbers you can trust?
options: Profile mode on a real device
questions.explanation: Profile is compiled like release but keeps the measuring tools. And it has to be a real device: a simulator runs on your computer's processor, which is far faster than a phone's, so the numbers flatter you.
whyWrong: Debug is several times slower and a simulator is far faster than a phone. Both errors at once.
Release has no measuring tools, and prints change the timing they are measuring.
A real device is right, but debug mode makes the numbers meaningless.

questions.prompt: What does `RepaintBoundary` do?
options: Puts the subtree on its own layer, so it is not redrawn with its neighbours
questions.explanation: It separates painting, not building. When something next to it repaints, the content inside the boundary is reused rather than drawn again. Right for something expensive and static next to something animating — and not worth scattering, because each boundary costs memory.
whyWrong: Rebuilding is Dart work and is unaffected: it is about painting.
It changes nothing about constraints or layout.
`const` is a different mechanism entirely.

questions.prompt: Why is the expensive widget passed as `child` rather than created inside the builder?
questions.code:
AnimatedBuilder(
  animation: controller,
  builder: (context, child) => Transform.rotate(
    angle: controller.value,
    child: child,
  ),
  child: const ExpensiveWidget(),
)
options: So that only the child is rotated
It is built once, not on every tick
questions.explanation: The `builder` runs on every tick of the animation — sixty times a second. Anything created in there is created sixty times a second. The `child` is built once, outside, and simply handed to the builder, which wraps it. It is the standard optimisation for any animated builder.
whyWrong: It is optional. It exists precisely for this optimisation.
What gets rotated is decided by where you put it in the `Transform`, not by this.
No boundary is created: that is a separate widget.

questions.prompt: How do you call a native iOS API from Dart?
options: A MethodChannel: invokeMethod on the Dart side, a handler in Swift
questions.explanation: A channel is the bridge between the two worlds: Dart sends a message with a method name, the native side handles it and replies. The call is always asynchronous, because it crosses that boundary.
whyWrong: Dart cannot import native frameworks: they are different worlds.
An isolate is still Dart. It gets you no closer to native code.
`compute` runs Dart elsewhere. It has nothing to do with the platform.

questions.prompt: You want a continuous stream of events from a native sensor. Which channel?
questions.explanation: `EventChannel` exists for exactly this: the native side sends events when they happen, and on the Dart side you get a `Stream`. Polling asks sixty times a minute for something that may have changed once, which wastes battery and arrives late.
whyWrong: Polling is the thing `EventChannel` was made to replace.
It can carry messages but has no stream semantics: you would be rebuilding `EventChannel` by hand.
A timer in Dart is polling again, with the same problems.

questions.prompt: In a widget test, what is the difference between `pump()` and `pumpAndSettle()`?
options: pump advances one frame; pumpAndSettle advances until nothing is animating
pumpAndSettle only exists in integration tests
questions.explanation: `pump` is for a change that takes effect immediately. `pumpAndSettle` is for after something that animates — a navigation, a dialog — so you wait until it has finished. With an endless animation it never returns, which is a confusing test to debug.
whyWrong: They behave quite differently, and using the wrong one gives you a test that fails for no obvious reason.
Both are available in ordinary widget tests.
Neither waits for the network: that is handled separately, usually with a fake.

questions.prompt: Which kind of test runs on a real device and checks a whole flow?
questions.explanation: It runs the real app on a real device, with real plugins and real navigation. It is the slowest kind, so you keep few of them — for the handful of flows that must never break, such as login and checkout.
whyWrong: A unit test is pure Dart with no widgets at all.
A widget test builds one widget in a fake environment, with no device.
A golden test compares a rendering with a saved image. It is about appearance.

questions.prompt: A list of ten thousand items stutters while scrolling. What is the first fix?
options: `ListView.builder`, so only the visible items are built
questions.explanation: `ListView.builder` builds only what is on screen plus a little margin, so ten thousand items cost the same as twenty. Anything that builds all of them up front will stutter whatever else you do.
whyWrong: That builds all ten thousand immediately, which is the worst case.
`shrinkWrap` forces every item to be laid out so the list can measure itself: it makes it worse.
A boundary separates painting. It does not stop ten thousand widgets being built.

questions.prompt: You change the code in `initState` and hot reload. What happens?
options: It does not run again: you need a hot restart
questions.explanation: Hot reload keeps the state, and `initState` only runs when the state is created. The new code is in the app but has not been executed, so nothing seems to change — which is why this quietly wastes people's time. A hot restart recreates everything.
whyWrong: It would only run again if the state were recreated, and hot reload deliberately does not do that.
Nothing crashes: the app carries on with the old values.
Nothing is automatic: you have to ask for the restart.

topics.title: Organising a large app
topics.summary: How to lay out a project so that six months and five people later it is still possible to change something without breaking three other things.

lesson.heading: Organise by feature, not by type
lesson.body:
The first thing people do is group files by what they **are**: all the models together, all the screens together, all the services together. It looks tidy and it falls apart quickly.

The reason is simple: **nobody ever works on "all the models"**. You work on checkout, or on search. With a layout by type, a single change means touching four folders, and finding everything that belongs to one feature means searching the whole project. Deleting a feature cleanly becomes impossible, so dead code stays for years.

**Feature-first** turns it round: one folder per feature, and inside it everything that feature needs. A change stays in one place, a new person can be shown one folder, and deleting a feature is deleting a folder.

What stays shared goes in `core`: networking, storage, the design system, error handling — the things that genuinely belong to no single feature.

The test for whether you have it right: **can you delete a feature by deleting its folder?** If removing checkout means hunting through six other directories, the boundaries are in the wrong place.
lesson.code:
// Feature-first: everything a feature needs, in one place
lib/
  core/              // networking, storage, theme, errors
  features/
    catalog/
      domain/        // entities, repository interfaces, use cases
      data/          // DTOs, APIs, implementations
      presentation/  // widgets and state holders
    checkout/
      domain/ data/ presentation/
  app.dart           // the router, and where everything is wired together

// By type: tidy-looking, and every change touches four folders
// lib/models/  lib/screens/  lib/services/  lib/widgets/

lesson.heading: The three layers, and which way they point
lesson.body:
Inside a feature, three layers, each with one job.

**Domain** — the business rules and the types they work on. Pure Dart: **no Flutter, no HTTP, no database**. An order knows whether it can be refunded; it knows nothing about how it was fetched or how it will be shown.

**Data** — where things come from. Clients, DTOs, databases, implementations of the interfaces the domain declared.

**Presentation** — widgets and state holders. It shows what it is given and reports what the user did.

And the rule that makes it worth doing: **the dependencies point inwards**. Presentation knows the domain. Data knows the domain. **The domain knows nobody.**

That is what buys you the three things people claim for it and rarely get. The rules can be tested in milliseconds, with no device and no network. You can change the database or the whole interface without touching them. And when a rule is wrong, there is one obvious place to look.

The quickest way to check: **open a domain file and look at its imports**. If `package:flutter/material.dart` or an HTTP client is in there, something is in the wrong layer.

lesson.heading: Why the interface lives in the domain
lesson.body:
The repository interface going in the domain, with the implementation in data, looks backwards the first time you see it. The interface is about fetching, so surely it belongs with the fetching?

No — and this is **dependency inversion**, the one idea worth taking from Clean Architecture even if you take nothing else.

If the domain imported the data layer to use a repository, the rules would depend on the infrastructure: change from REST to GraphQL and the business logic has to be touched. By declaring the interface in the domain, you flip the arrow. The domain says what it needs; data provides it. The dependency now points inwards, like everything else.

Two things follow, and they are the practical payoff:

**You can test without any network.** Write a fake repository that returns whatever you want, and the rules can be tested exhaustively in milliseconds.

**You can change where data comes from without touching the rules.** REST to GraphQL, a cache added, an offline mode — all of it happens in data.

The other half of the boundary is the **DTO**. What the network sends you — snake_case, nullable everywhere, an id as a string that is really a number — should not become your domain type. A DTO holds that shape, and a mapper converts it at the edge. Then the day the API changes a field name, exactly one file changes.

lesson.heading: Packages, when folders stop being enough
lesson.body:
A folder is a suggestion. Nothing stops anyone importing across it, and in a hurry somebody will — and the boundary you drew is gone without anybody noticing.

An **internal package** makes it real. Put a feature in its own package, declare what it depends on in its `pubspec.yaml`, and an import that crosses the boundary **does not compile**. The rule is now enforced by the tool rather than by review.

What else you get: a package can be built and tested on its own, so its tests run in seconds; and in a CI setup, only the packages that changed need rebuilding.

What it costs: more files, a dependency graph to maintain, and a real nuisance when you have to move something between packages.

So the advice is **not** to start this way. Start with folders, and extract a package when two things are both true: **the boundary has stopped moving**, and there is a **concrete benefit** — a team that owns it, tests that are too slow, or something genuinely reused by two apps. Extracting too early means spending the cost before you have earned the benefit, and then fighting the structure every time the design changes.

lesson.heading: The design system
lesson.body:
Colours and spacing scattered through the code is how an app slowly stops looking like one app. A brand colour written in fourteen places means fourteen places to change, and one of them gets missed.

The fix is a **design system**: the tokens — colours, spacing, text styles, corner radii — declared once, and used everywhere by name.

The Flutter way of doing it is **`ThemeExtension`**. It attaches your own tokens to the standard `ThemeData`, so they arrive through the same `Theme.of(context)` as everything else, they are typed, and they **interpolate** — which means they animate properly when the theme changes, including between light and dark.

Why not just a file of global constants? Because constants cannot vary with the theme. One set of constants means one theme for ever, and adding dark mode later means touching every usage.

Above the tokens sit the shared components: your button, your card, your empty state. The rule that keeps them useful: **a component in the design system must not know about any feature**. The moment your button imports something from checkout, it has stopped being shared.

questions.prompt: Where does a rule like "an order can be refunded only if it has not shipped" belong?
options: In the widget that shows the button
questions.explanation: It is a business rule, so it belongs in the domain, where it can be tested in milliseconds with no device. Put it in the widget and it can only be tested by building widgets — and it gets duplicated the moment a second screen needs the same answer.
whyWrong: Then the rule exists only where that button is, and the next screen reimplements it slightly differently.
The client fetches data. It should know nothing about what the data means.
The repository decides where data comes from, not what the business allows.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of organising by feature rather than by type?
options: A change stays in one folder, and a feature can be deleted
You do not have to write tests
questions.explanation: Nobody works on "all the models": they work on checkout. With a feature-first layout a change touches one folder, a new person can be shown one folder, and removing a feature is removing a folder.
whyWrong: The number of files is roughly the same: what changes is where they are.
Startup time has nothing to do with how the source is arranged.
The tests are the same. They just live next to what they test.

questions.prompt: Which import in a domain file tells you something is in the wrong layer?
questions.explanation: The domain holds the rules and must not know about the interface. Importing Flutter means a widget has crept into the rules — or the rules have crept into a widget. Either way, something has to move.
whyWrong: `dart:async` is pure Dart: a `Future` in a domain interface is completely normal.
`dart:math` is pure Dart too, and a rule may well need it.
Domain files importing each other is exactly what they should do.

questions.prompt: Why does the repository interface go in the domain rather than in the data layer?
options: It is a convention of typed languages
So the domain does not depend on the infrastructure
Because data cannot declare abstract classes
questions.explanation: This is dependency inversion. The domain declares what it needs; data provides it. So the arrow points inwards, and changing from REST to GraphQL, or adding a cache, happens entirely in data without the rules being touched.
whyWrong: It is not a convention: it is the thing that keeps the rules independent.
It can declare them perfectly well. The question is which layer should own the contract.
The number of files is the same. What changes is which way the dependency points.

questions.prompt: Why keep DTOs separate from domain entities?
options: So that a change in the API format stops at the boundary
Because entities cannot have final fields
questions.explanation: The network's shape — snake_case, nullable everywhere, an id that is a string — should not become your domain's shape. Keep them separate with a mapper at the edge, and the day the API renames a field, one file changes.
whyWrong: DTOs exist precisely to be serialised.
It is the opposite: you write a mapper on purpose, and that is what buys you the isolation.
They can, and usually should.

questions.prompt: What does an internal package give you that a folder does not?
questions.explanation: A folder is a suggestion: nothing stops an import crossing it. A package declares its dependencies, so an import that crosses the boundary does not compile. The rule is enforced by the tool instead of by whoever reviews the change.
whyWrong: The compiled code is the same: this is about organisation, not speed.
Hot reload is usually slightly slower with many packages, not faster.
They all share the project's SDK constraints.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this widget?
options: The presentation layer knows about HTTP and the API's format
Dio must always be used with await
questions.explanation: Three boundaries broken at once: the widget knows the URL, the HTTP client and the JSON's shape. It cannot be tested without a network, and the day the API changes a field name, a widget has to be edited. A repository in the middle fixes all three.
whyWrong: It works in a stateless widget. The real problem here is a layering one.
The missing generic is untidy but not the actual fault.
`FutureBuilder` takes the future and awaits it for you. That part is fine.

questions.prompt: In a layered architecture, which way do the dependencies point?
options: Domain depends on data, which depends on presentation
Each layer depends on the one below, in a chain
Presentation and data both depend on the domain
questions.explanation: The rules sit at the centre and know nothing about the database or the screen. That is what lets you test them without a device and change either side without touching them. The arrows point inwards, towards the domain.
whyWrong: That is upside down: the rules would then depend on the infrastructure.
A chain would make the domain depend on data, which is exactly what is being avoided.
Core holds shared tools. Depending on it is normal, but it does not describe the direction between the layers.

questions.prompt: When is it worth extracting a feature into its own package?
options: Straight away, before writing any code
When the boundary has stopped moving and the extraction buys something concrete
Only above a hundred thousand lines
Never: internal packages are not used in Flutter
questions.explanation: A package costs files, a dependency graph and real friction when something has to move. It pays off when the boundary is settled and there is a reason — a team that owns it, tests that are too slow, something genuinely shared between two apps.
whyWrong: Before writing the code you do not know where the boundaries are, so you will draw them wrong.
There is no threshold in lines: it depends on stability and on the benefit.
They are widely used, especially in large projects and monorepos.

questions.prompt: How do you expose design tokens — brand colours, spacing — to the whole app?
options: A hand-written InheritedWidget for each one
questions.explanation: A `ThemeExtension` attaches your tokens to the standard theme: they arrive through `Theme.of(context)`, they are typed, and they interpolate — so they animate correctly when the theme changes, including between light and dark.
whyWrong: Constants cannot vary with the theme, so dark mode means touching every usage.
That is reinventing by hand what `ThemeExtension` already provides, with no interpolation.
Passing them down means every widget has to carry them, and the one you forget is the one that looks wrong.

topics.title: Talking to the platform
topics.summary: Flutter draws its own screens, so for anything the phone itself owns — the battery, a native map, a C library — you have to go and ask. Here is how the asking works.

lesson.heading: Why you ever need to leave Dart
lesson.body:
Flutter draws every pixel itself. That is its strength and also its boundary: your Dart code lives in its own little world, and the phone's own features — the battery level, a payments SDK, HealthKit, a native map — are not in it.

So there has to be a door. In Flutter that door is called a **channel**, and it works like sending a letter rather than calling a function.

You send a **message**: the name of what you want, plus some arguments. Flutter turns that into bytes (that is **serialization** — packing a value into a stream of bytes), hands it to the native side, which unpacks it, does the work, packs the answer, and sends it back.

Two consequences follow from "it is a letter", and they are the two things people get wrong:

**Every call is asynchronous.** You always `await`. There is no synchronous version, because the reply has to travel.

**Only simple things fit in the envelope.** Numbers, strings, booleans, lists, maps, byte buffers. **Not your objects.** A `User` has to be flattened into a map and rebuilt on the other side.

There are three kinds of channel, and the names say what they carry:

- **`MethodChannel`** — "do this and tell me the answer". One call, one reply. This is the common case.
- **`EventChannel`** — "keep telling me". A stream from native to Dart: location updates, connectivity, sensors.
- **`BasicMessageChannel`** — plain messages in both directions, no method names. Rarely needed.

lesson.heading: The Dart side, and the three ways it can go
lesson.body:
On the native side you register a **handler**: a function that receives the method name and the arguments, and replies in one of exactly three ways.

**`result.success(value)`** — it worked, here is the answer.

**`result.error(code, message, details)`** — it failed, and here is why. In Dart this arrives as a **`PlatformException`** being thrown, with that same code and message. Use it for real failures: permission denied, the device cannot do it.

**`result.notImplemented()`** — I do not know that method name. In Dart it arrives as a `MissingPluginException`, which is almost always the symptom of a typo in a method name, or of a channel registered on one platform and forgotten on the other.

The rule that catches people: **you must reply exactly once.** Reply twice and the platform throws; never reply and the Dart `await` hangs for ever — no error, no timeout, just a spinner that never stops. In a handler with several branches, check that every single path ends in one of the three.

One more thing worth knowing, because it causes mysterious freezes: the handler runs on the **platform's main thread** — the UI thread of the native side. Do slow work there and you freeze the native UI, which on iOS is also what gets your app killed by the watchdog. Anything slow goes on a background queue or a coroutine, and only the reply comes back to the main thread.

lesson.heading: When native code has to keep talking: EventChannel
lesson.body:
A `MethodChannel` answers once. For something that keeps happening — the accelerometer, connectivity changing, a download's progress — you want an **`EventChannel`**, which in Dart looks like an ordinary `Stream`.

The native side implements two callbacks:

**`onListen`** — someone in Dart has started listening: start the sensor, register the observer. You are handed a **sink**, the thing you push values into.

**`onCancel`** — nobody is listening any more: stop the sensor, remove the observer.

`onCancel` is the one that gets forgotten, and forgetting it is a battery leak: the GPS stays on after the screen that wanted it is gone. The pairing to keep in your head is **start in `onListen`, stop in `onCancel`**, and on the Dart side, cancel the subscription in `dispose`.

The tempting alternative is a `MethodChannel` polled on a timer. Don't: you get values late, you burn battery asking when nothing has changed, and you still miss events between polls. Push beats poll whenever the native side knows when something happened.

lesson.heading: Pigeon: letting a tool write the boring half
lesson.body:
Hand-written channels have one real weakness: **nothing checks that the two sides agree**. The method name is a string, the arguments are an untyped map. Rename a method in Swift and Dart still compiles happily — and then crashes on a device, for a user.

**Pigeon** removes that whole class of bug. You describe the interface once, in a Dart file that is only a description, and Pigeon generates the Dart, the Swift and the Kotlin. Now a mismatch is a **compile error**, not a crash report.

It uses two annotations, and the direction is the thing to remember:

**`@HostApi`** — Dart calls native. ("Host" is the platform.)

**`@FlutterApi`** — native calls Dart.

So the guidance: hand-write a channel for one quick call; use Pigeon the moment the interface has several methods or real data types, which in practice means any plugin you intend to keep.

And when you package it up as a plugin, you will meet the **federated** layout. It looks like bureaucracy and it exists for one reason: so that someone can add Windows support without touching your iOS code. There is an `_platform_interface` package declaring the contract, one package per platform implementing it, and the main package that depends on them. Everyone implements the same interface, nobody edits anyone else's code.

lesson.heading: PlatformView and FFI: the two heavier doors
lesson.body:
Two more tools, each for a case channels cannot cover.

**PlatformView** — when you need a real native view inside a Flutter screen: a MapKit map, a camera preview, a WebView, an ad. `UiKitView` on iOS, `AndroidView` on Android. The thing you are placing is a genuine native view, not something Flutter drew.

The cost is real and worth understanding. Flutter normally composes its whole scene by itself; a native view has to be **stitched into** that scene, which means synchronising two rendering systems and adding layers. One map is fine. A long scrolling list with a native view per row will stutter. So: use one when you must, and never put one in a list row if a Flutter widget would do.

**`dart:ffi`** — when you want to call a **C** library directly: a crypto routine, an image codec, a database engine. No channel, no serialization, and crucially **no `await`**: the call is synchronous, like calling a function, because there is no message being sent.

What you take on in exchange is **manual memory management**. Dart's garbage collector knows nothing about memory you allocated on the C side. You allocate with `calloc`, and **you** free it — and the practical way to not get this wrong is an `Arena`, which frees everything in the block when the block ends. Forget to free and you have a leak the GC will never clean up; free twice and you crash.

The last thing, easy to miss until the end of a project: **FFI and PlatformView do not exist on the web**, and nor do platform channels in the usual sense. If web is a target, everything native needs a path that does not use them.

questions.prompt: Are calls on a `MethodChannel` synchronous or asynchronous?
options: Synchronous: the result comes back immediately
Synchronous on iOS, asynchronous on Android
questions.explanation: A channel call is a message: it is packed into bytes, sent across, unpacked, answered, and sent back. That journey takes time, so the result always arrives as a `Future` and you always `await` it.
whyWrong: There is no synchronous version. For a genuinely synchronous call you need `dart:ffi`, which sends no message at all.
The mechanism is the same on both: a message that travels.
The codec decides how values are packed, not whether you have to wait.

questions.prompt: You need to show a native map (MapKit / Google Maps SDK) inside a Flutter screen. What do you use?
questions.explanation: The map is a real native view, with its own gestures and its own rendering. A PlatformView places that actual view inside the Flutter scene, which is the only way to get it with its behaviour intact.
whyWrong: Shipping pixels over a channel every frame would be far too slow, and you would lose every gesture.
FFI calls C functions. It cannot place a view on screen.
A `CustomPainter` draws with Flutter. You would be reimplementing a mapping SDK by hand.

questions.prompt: What is Pigeon for?
options: Speeding up channels with a custom binary codec
Generating typed code for both sides of the channel
Automatically converting an Android plugin into an iOS one
questions.explanation: By hand, a channel's method name is a string and its arguments are an untyped map, so nothing checks that Dart and Swift agree. Pigeon generates both sides from one description, which turns a mismatch into a compile error instead of a crash on someone's phone.
whyWrong: Speed is not the point: the generated code uses the same transport.
The Swift still runs natively. Pigeon only generates the code that calls across.
It generates the scaffolding for each platform. The actual native implementations you still write.

questions.prompt: What happens if the native side replies with an error and you don't catch anything in Dart?
questions.code: final level = await channel.invokeMethod<int>('batteryLevel');
questions.explanation: `result.error(...)` on the native side becomes a thrown `PlatformException` in Dart, carrying the same code and message. Uncaught, it propagates like any other exception — so wrap the call in `try`/`catch` and decide what the user should see.
whyWrong: `null` means a reply of `success(null)`. An error throws instead.
Nothing retries for you: retries are something you write.
Nothing quits. An exception is thrown, and your error handling decides what happens next.

questions.prompt: Which thread does a `MethodChannel`'s native handler run on?
options: A background thread chosen by Flutter
The same Dart isolate that made the call
questions.explanation: The handler runs on the native side's UI thread. That is why slow work there freezes the native interface — and on iOS gets the app killed by the watchdog. Put anything slow on a background queue and come back to the main thread only to reply.
whyWrong: Flutter does not move you to a background thread: doing that is your job.
The raster thread draws frames. Channel handlers have nothing to do with it.
The isolate is Dart's side. The handler is native code, on a native thread.

questions.prompt: Native code needs to send Dart continuous accelerometer updates. Which channel?
questions.explanation: An `EventChannel` is exactly this: the native side pushes values as they happen and Dart receives a `Stream`. You start the sensor in `onListen` and — the part people forget — stop it in `onCancel`.
whyWrong: Polling arrives late, burns battery asking when nothing changed, and still misses events between polls.
It would work, but you would be hand-building the streaming that `EventChannel` already gives you.
A PlatformView is for showing a native view. It is not a transport for data.

questions.prompt: Main advantage of `dart:ffi` over a platform channel?
options: It also works on the web
It doesn't require any native code
questions.explanation: FFI calls a C function directly: nothing is packed into bytes and nothing travels, so the call is synchronous and the overhead is close to a normal function call. The price is that the memory is yours to free.
whyWrong: FFI does not exist on the web. If web is a target you need another path entirely.
The opposite: the garbage collector knows nothing about C memory, so you free it yourself — an `Arena` is the safe way.
There has to be a C library. FFI is how you reach it, not a way to avoid it.

questions.prompt: In a federated plugin, what is the `platform_interface` package for?
options: Holding the iOS and Android implementations
Defining the contract every platform implementation must honor
Registering the plugin with the engine
questions.explanation: It holds the contract and nothing else. That is what lets somebody add Windows support in a separate package, implementing the same interface, without touching your iOS or Android code.
whyWrong: Those live in their own packages. Keeping them out of the contract is the whole point.
Publishing is a command you run, not something a package does.
Registration happens in each platform package, where the native code is.

questions.prompt: Why can a long list of PlatformViews degrade performance?
options: Because Flutter rebuilds them from scratch every frame
Because they always use software rendering
Because each native view spins up an isolate
Because compositing native views with the Flutter scene costs synchronization and extra layers
questions.explanation: Flutter normally composes its whole scene itself. Each native view has to be stitched into that scene, which means synchronising two rendering systems and adding layers. One is fine; one per row in a scrolling list stutters.
whyWrong: They are not rebuilt each frame. The cost is in combining two rendering systems.
They render natively, hardware-accelerated. The cost is the compositing, not the rendering.
No isolate is created: an isolate is a Dart thing and a native view is not Dart.

questions.prompt: With `dart:ffi` you allocate a buffer with `calloc<Uint8>(n)`. Who frees it?
options: Dart's garbage collector, once the `Pointer` is no longer reachable
You do, with `calloc.free` or by using an `Arena`
The C library, when the function returns
Nobody: native memory is released when the isolate shuts down
questions.explanation: The garbage collector manages Dart objects, and native memory is not one. You free it yourself — and an `Arena` is the way not to get it wrong, since it frees everything when the block ends, even if something threw.
whyWrong: The collector never sees that memory: the `Pointer` is just a number to it.
Only if its documentation says so. Memory you allocated is yours to free.
It is released when the process ends, which is far too late: until then it is a leak.

topics.title: Getting the app out
topics.summary: Signing, flavours, secrets and the two stores: what stands between a build on your machine and an app on somebody's phone.

lesson.heading: Signing: what it is, before how it works
lesson.body:
A phone will not run just any app. Before it installs anything it wants proof of **who made it**, and that the file has not been altered since. That proof is a **signature**: a cryptographic stamp made with a **private key** only you hold.

The whole subject is confusing mostly because Apple and Google use different words for the same idea. So here is the idea first: **one secret key, which signs; and something public that says the key is yours.**

On **iOS** that "something public" is a **certificate** issued by Apple, and it comes with a second piece, the **provisioning profile** — a file that ties together three things: which app (the bundle ID), which certificate may sign it, and what it is allowed to do (push notifications, iCloud, and so on).

So an iOS release needs: a distribution certificate, a matching private key in your keychain, and a profile whose bundle ID is exactly your app's. The classic error — *"no profile matching the bundle identifier"* — almost always means the bundle ID in Xcode and the one in the profile differ by a character.

On **Android** it is simpler to describe: you have a **keystore**, a file holding the private key, protected by passwords. That is it: no profile, no certificate from Google.

And one rule that matters more than everything else here: **if you lose the Android keystore, you can no longer update the app.** Google will not accept an update signed by a different key, because from the phone's point of view it is a different app from a different author. Back up the keystore somewhere you will still have it in three years.

lesson.heading: Keeping the key out of the repository
lesson.body:
Gradle needs the keystore's passwords in order to sign. The obvious move is to write them in `build.gradle`, and it is the one thing you must not do: **everything in the repository is readable by everyone who can clone it**, for ever, including in the history after you "remove" it.

The pattern instead: the passwords live in a `key.properties` file which is **gitignored**, Gradle reads them from there, and on a build server the file is created from **secrets** — values stored by the CI system, encrypted, visible to nobody.

It is worth knowing how Google's side of this works too, because it changes what you are protecting. With **Play App Signing**, Google holds the real signing key. You sign with an **upload key** and upload; Google verifies it, strips your signature and **re-signs** with the app key it keeps. Two keys with two jobs: the upload key proves it is you uploading, the app key is what phones actually check.

The good part is that the key that matters cannot be lost — Google has it. And if your upload key is compromised or lost, Google can reset it, which is exactly what used to be unrecoverable.

On iOS, the team version of the same problem is **`fastlane match`**: certificates and profiles kept encrypted in a shared repository, and `match` installs the same ones on every machine and on CI. Without it, everyone generates their own certificates, hits the limit, revokes someone else's, and a build breaks on a Friday.

lesson.heading: Flavours: several apps from one codebase
lesson.body:
You want the app pointing at a test server on your phone, and the real one in the store — and you want **both installed at the same time**, because testing a staging build by uninstalling the real one is miserable.

Two apps can only coexist on a phone if they have **different identifiers**. That is what a **flavour** is for: one codebase, several variants, each with its own bundle ID, its own name on the home screen, its own icon, its own endpoint.

The convention that works: `dev` against local or staging, with the name "App Dev" and a differently coloured icon so a screenshot is never ambiguous; `staging` against the pre-production server, for whoever tests; `prod`, the real one.

Flavours are configured where each platform expects it — `productFlavors` in Gradle on Android, schemes and configurations in Xcode on iOS — and then selected on the command line with `--flavor`.

The other half is the **entry point**: `-t lib/main_dev.dart`. A separate `main` per flavour, each one setting up what differs — which crash reporting, which logging, which analytics — and then calling the same shared `runApp`. Keep the duplication to those few lines; everything else stays in one place.

lesson.heading: Configuration and secrets: two different problems
lesson.body:
The values that change between variants — the API URL, which analytics key, whether a debug menu is on — come in with **`--dart-define`** and are read with **`String.fromEnvironment`**.

There is one trap here, and it catches everybody once. These values are resolved **at compile time**, which means the read must be **`const`**:

```
const apiUrl = String.fromEnvironment('API_URL');   // works
final apiUrl = String.fromEnvironment('API_URL');   // always empty
```

With `final`, the compiler cannot substitute the value and you silently get the default — an empty string. No error, no warning: the app simply talks to nothing. Always `const`, and always a sensible `defaultValue`.

Now the part that is not about configuration at all. **A secret cannot live in the app.** Not in the code, not in a `--dart-define`, not in a file in the assets, not obfuscated. An app installed on a phone is a file somebody owns: it can be unzipped, decompiled, and watched while it runs. Every string in it, including every key, is recoverable.

So the rule: **anything that must stay secret stays on your server.** The app asks the server, the server holds the key and talks to the paid service. Keys that are *meant* to be public — a Maps key locked to your bundle ID, a Firebase config — can ship, because they were designed to be seen and are restricted on the other end.

lesson.heading: Obfuscation, symbols, and automating the release
lesson.body:
**Obfuscation** renames your classes and methods to meaningless short names. It does not make the app secure — a determined person still gets through — it just raises the cost of casually reading your logic.

The consequence is the thing to remember, because people discover it at the worst moment. Once the names are gone, a **crash report becomes unreadable**: you get `a.b(c.dart:1)` instead of `CheckoutPage.pay`. Which is why the two flags always travel together:

**`--obfuscate`** renames; **`--split-debug-info=<dir>`** writes out a **symbol file**, the map from the short names back to the real ones.

That directory is now precious. Upload it to your crash service with every release, and **keep it**, filed per version — a crash in version 1.4 can only be read with 1.4's symbols. Lose them and the crashes from that release are permanently unreadable.

The stores want different things: iOS takes an **`.ipa`** (and the upload goes to App Store Connect, usually via TestFlight first); Android wants an **App Bundle**, `.aab`. A bundle is not an installable app — it is everything needed to build one, and the Play Store generates a tailored APK per device, with only the right screen densities and the right processor architecture. Which is why the download is smaller than a universal APK, and why an `.apk` is now only for testing and sideloading.

Finally, automate it. A release done by hand is a release where one step gets forgotten, and the forgotten step is usually the symbols. The job of CI here is: run the tests, build the signed artefact, upload it, upload the symbols, tag the commit — the same way every time, so a release is boring.

questions.prompt: What do you need to sign a distributable iOS build?
options: A distribution certificate and a provisioning profile consistent with the bundle ID
questions.explanation: The certificate says the signing key is yours; the profile ties that certificate to one bundle ID and a set of capabilities. If the bundle ID differs from the app's by a single character, the build fails.
whyWrong: The Apple ID gets you into the account. It is not what signs the binary.
A keystore is the Android mechanism. iOS uses certificates and profiles.
TestFlight distributes a build that is already signed. It does not sign it.

questions.prompt: Which format does the Play Store require today to publish an app?
options: Either an APK or an AAB
questions.explanation: An App Bundle is not an installable app: it is everything needed to build one. The store then generates a tailored APK per device — only the right densities, only the right processor architecture — so the download is smaller.
whyWrong: A universal APK carries every density and architecture for every device, and the store no longer accepts one for a new app.
Splitting by hand is what the bundle does for you, and better, since it also splits by density and language.
An APK is still fine for testing and sideloading, but not for publishing.

questions.prompt: Where do you keep `key.properties` and the release keystore?
options: In the repository, so CI can find them
Outside the repository, injected as secrets on CI
Inside `assets/`, so Dart can read them
questions.explanation: Anything in the repository is readable by everyone who can clone it, including in the history after you delete it. Keep them out, gitignore the file, and let CI write it from encrypted secrets.
whyWrong: CI finds them through its secrets. Committing them hands your signing key to anyone with repository access.
`assets/` ships inside the app, so you would be handing the key to every user.
`res/` also ships inside the app, and is trivially readable by unzipping it.

questions.prompt: What is a flavor for?
options: Choosing between JIT and AOT compilation
Creating variants of the app (dev, staging, prod) with different IDs, names, and endpoints
questions.explanation: Different identifiers are what let two variants live on the same phone, so you can test staging without uninstalling the real app. The flavour also carries the name, the icon and which server it talks to.
whyWrong: That is decided by debug versus release, not by the flavour.
Size comes from the build mode and from tree shaking. A flavour changes neither.
Translations are localisation, and are the same across every flavour.

questions.prompt: How do you pass the API URL so it changes between staging and production?
options: With a `.env` file bundled in the assets
By changing it by hand before each build
questions.explanation: `--dart-define` sets the value at build time and `String.fromEnvironment` reads it — remembering that the read has to be `const`, or you silently get the default.
whyWrong: `kDebugMode` only distinguishes debug from release. A release build against staging would be impossible.
A file in the assets ships inside the app, readable by anyone who unzips it, and still has to be edited per build.
That works until the evening someone ships to the store with the staging URL still in place.

questions.prompt: With Play App Signing, what's the difference between the upload key and the app signing key?
options: They're the same key under two names
The upload key signs debug builds, the other signs release builds
You sign with the upload key, and Google re-signs with the app key it holds
The upload key is only used for the first release
questions.explanation: Two keys, two jobs: the upload key proves to Google that the upload is from you, and the app key — which Google keeps — is what phones actually verify. The benefit is that the key that matters cannot be lost, and a compromised upload key can be reset.
whyWrong: They are genuinely different keys, held by different parties.
Debug builds are signed by a local debug key and never go near the store.
You use it for every upload, not just the first.

questions.prompt: In release, this variable is always empty. Why?
questions.code:
final apiUrl = String.fromEnvironment('API_URL');
// build: flutter build apk --dart-define=API_URL=https://api.app.io
options: Because the name must be lowercase
Because the read isn't `const`: the value is resolved at compile time
questions.explanation: `fromEnvironment` is substituted by the compiler, so it only works in a `const` context. With `final` you silently get the default — an empty string, no error and no warning. Change it to `const` and add a `defaultValue`.
whyWrong: It works in both. The mode is not the problem.
A missing default is why the result is empty rather than something sensible, but the cause is the missing `const`.
The name is just a string: case does not matter as long as the two sides match.

questions.prompt: You ship with `--obfuscate --split-debug-info`. What does that mean for crash reports?
options: Stack traces are unreadable unless you upload the symbols to your crash service
Only native crashes come out obfuscated
questions.explanation: Obfuscation removes the real names, so a trace arrives as `a.b(c.dart:1)`. The symbol file written by `--split-debug-info` is the map back, so upload it with every release and keep it filed per version.
whyWrong: They stay readable only if the symbols are uploaded. Obfuscation is exactly the removal of those names.
They are recorded as always. What changes is whether you can read them.
It is the Dart names that are obfuscated. Native crashes need their own dSYM or mapping.

questions.prompt: Can the private key for a paid service live in the app if the binary is obfuscated?
options: No: the binary can be inspected, so the secret belongs on the backend
Yes, if you save it to the keychain on first launch
questions.explanation: An installed app is a file somebody owns: it can be unzipped, decompiled and watched while it runs. Every string in it is recoverable. The key stays on your server, and the app asks the server.
whyWrong: Obfuscation renames code. The string with the key is still in the binary.
`--dart-define` writes the value into the binary at build time. Same binary, same string.
The keychain protects it on that device, but the key had to be in the app to get there.

questions.prompt: What problem does `fastlane match` solve on a team?
options: It keeps iOS certificates and profiles encrypted in a shared repo and installs the same ones everywhere
It builds the AAB and uploads it to the Play Store
It runs integration tests before the build
questions.explanation: Without it, everyone generates their own certificates, the account hits its limit, somebody revokes somebody else's, and a build breaks. `match` keeps one encrypted set and installs it on every machine and on CI.
whyWrong: That is `supply` (or `gradle` plus an upload lane). `match` only deals with signing.
That is `increment_build_number`, a different action.
Tests are `scan`. `match` runs nothing.

topics.title: Living with an app in the wild
topics.summary: Once it is published you cannot watch over anyone's shoulder. What you need instead: seeing the crashes, being able to switch a feature off, opening the right screen from a link, and working with no signal.

lesson.heading: Seeing what breaks
lesson.body:
On your own phone, an error is a red screen and a stack trace in the console. On a stranger's phone it is nothing — unless you arranged, in advance, for it to be sent to you.

That is what a **crash reporting service** is: a library that catches the error, packages it with the stack trace, the device, the version and the recent breadcrumbs, and sends it somewhere you can read it.

Flutter needs **two** hooks, because errors arrive by two different routes, and wiring up only one is the common mistake:

**`FlutterError.onError`** — errors inside the framework: a bad build, a layout that cannot be measured, an exception in a widget.

**`PlatformDispatcher.instance.onError`** — everything else: an error in an async callback, a failed `Future` nobody awaited, anything outside a widget.

Both of them, always. And `runApp` inside a **`runZonedGuarded`** if you also want errors from zones you spawned.

On **logging**: `print` is not a logging system. It has no levels, so you cannot filter; it goes nowhere you can read later; and it is **visible on the device** — on Android, anyone can read your logs with `adb logcat`, so a `print` of a response body is a data leak.

What to use instead: a logger with levels (debug / info / warning / error), verbose only in debug builds, and in release only what you actually need, with **no personal data and no tokens** in it. A useful habit: log the *shape* of a failure, never its contents — "login failed, status 401" and not the request body.

lesson.heading: The four numbers worth watching
lesson.body:
A dashboard with forty graphs gets looked at twice. Four numbers get looked at every day, and these are the four that tell you whether the app is well.

**Crash-free users** — the percentage of people who used the app today without it crashing. One number, and the most honest one you have. A healthy app sits above 99.5%. The reason to watch *users* and not *crashes* is that one person crashing in a loop two hundred times would otherwise look like a catastrophe.

**ANR / frozen frames** — the app is not crashing, it is **stuck**. Often worse for the person using it than a crash, which at least ends. Android reports ANRs ("application not responding") directly.

**Cold start time** — from tap to something useful on screen. It is the first thing anyone experiences, and the first thing they judge.

**The failure rate of your own API calls** — because half of the "app is broken" reports are actually a backend being slow or returning errors.

The two habits that make these numbers useful rather than decorative:

**Always break them down by app version.** An average across versions hides exactly the thing you need to see: that the release you shipped yesterday is the one that is broken.

**Set an alert on the one that matters**, so that a bad release finds you rather than you finding it on Monday.

lesson.heading: Being able to turn something off without shipping
lesson.body:
A release takes a day to review and then days to reach people. So if a feature is broken, "ship a fix" is far too slow — some users will be on the broken version for a week.

A **feature flag** is the answer: a value fetched from the server that decides whether a feature is on. It turns a code change into a **configuration change**, which takes effect in minutes and needs no review.

Three things it buys you. A **kill switch** — the broken thing goes off now, for everyone. A **gradual rollout** — on for 5% of users, watch the crash numbers, then 50%, then everyone. And an **A/B test** — two versions at once, compared on real behaviour instead of opinion.

There is one detail everybody gets wrong the first time, and it shows up as a bug report from the very first launch. Fetching the config is a **network call**, so on the first run it has not finished yet, and the flag has whatever **default** you compiled in.

So: always set the defaults before anything reads a flag, and make the default the **safe** value — the old behaviour. If a flag defaults to "on" and the network is unavailable, you have shipped the new feature to everyone with no way to turn it off.

And read a flag **once per session**, into a value, rather than at every `build`. A flag that changes mid-session gives you an interface that rearranges itself under someone's thumb.

lesson.heading: Links and notifications: arriving from outside
lesson.body:
Two ways in that both end with the same question — which screen, with what state — and both are where routing bugs live.

A **deep link** is a link that opens the app on the right screen. There are two kinds, and the difference matters:

A **custom scheme** — `myapp://order/42` — is easy and weak: any app can claim the same scheme, and in a browser the link means nothing.

A **universal link** (iOS) or **app link** (Android) is a normal `https://` URL that opens your app. It is stronger because it is **verified**: you publish a file on your domain (`apple-app-site-association` / `assetlinks.json`) that names your app, and the system checks it. Nobody else can hijack your domain's links — and if the app is not installed, the same URL just opens the website. Declaring an intent filter alone is not enough: without that published file, Android shows the chooser instead.

For **push notifications**, the one thing that surprises people is the **token**: the address of that installation. It is not stable. It changes on reinstall, on restore to a new device, sometimes on an update. So: read it on every launch, listen to `onTokenRefresh`, and send it to your backend each time. A stale token is a notification delivered to nobody.

And the background handler is genuinely strange, so it is worth knowing why. When a push arrives with the app closed, Dart runs your handler in a **fresh isolate** — a separate little world with nothing initialised and none of your app's state. Hence the rules: it must be **top-level** (not a method, not a closure), it must be annotated **`@pragma('vm:entry-point')`** so that tree shaking — the compiler's removal of code nobody calls — does not delete it, and it must initialise anything it uses itself. Do the minimum there: store what arrived and get out.
