lesson.heading: No signal, and the first two seconds
lesson.body:
**Offline.** The instinct is to call the network and show an error when it fails. It works, and it makes an app that is useless on a train.

The arrangement that actually holds is to turn it round: the **local database is the source of truth**. The interface reads from the database, always, and therefore always has something to show. The network's job is only to **update** the database — and when the data arrives, the screen changes because the database changed.

For things the user *does* offline, a **queue**: the action is written down locally, applied to the local state immediately so the interface responds, and sent when there is signal.

That gives you two problems to decide on explicitly, because they will happen. **Conflicts** — somebody edited the same thing elsewhere; pick a rule and write it down (last write wins, or ask). And **ordering** — the queue must be sent in order, or a delete can arrive before the edit it was deleting.

**Startup.** Cold start is the first thing anyone judges, and it has one common cause: too much done before the first frame. Every SDK initialised in `main`, every awaited call, is time on a blank screen.

So: **measure first**, with `flutter run --trace-startup`, because guessing here is how you optimise the wrong thing. Then move everything that is not needed for the first frame to after it — analytics, crash reporting, anything remote — and only `await` what the first screen genuinely cannot be drawn without.

A splash screen does not make it faster. It only makes the wait less ugly, and that is a different problem from the one the numbers are showing you.

questions.prompt: What is a remotely fetched feature flag for?
options: Turning a feature on or off without a new release
Translating the app into multiple languages
questions.explanation: A release takes days to reach everyone, so "ship a fix" is too slow for something broken. A flag turns a code change into a configuration change: off in minutes, for everyone, with no review.
whyWrong: The code for both paths is still in the binary, so nothing gets smaller.
Fetching the config is a network call: if anything, it is work at startup, not a saving.
Translations are localisation, and ship with the app.

questions.prompt: Why isn't `print` a good logging system in production?
options: Because it's automatically stripped in release
Because it has no levels, doesn't reach any service, and can expose data
Because it blocks the event loop
Because it only works on Android
questions.explanation: No levels means you cannot filter; it goes nowhere you can read later; and on a device the output is readable — `adb logcat` on Android — so printing a response body is a data leak.
whyWrong: It is not stripped. It stays in the release build and keeps printing.
It does not block anything meaningfully. The problems are filtering, reach and privacy.
It works everywhere. That is part of why it is tempting.

questions.prompt: Which hooks do you need to capture errors in a Flutter app?
questions.explanation: Errors arrive by two routes: inside the framework, and everywhere else — async callbacks, unawaited `Future`s. You need both hooks, and installing only the first is the usual mistake.
whyWrong: `try`/`catch` only covers the points you thought of. The ones that matter are the ones you did not.
That misses everything outside the framework: an error in a callback would go unreported.
`ErrorWidget.builder` changes what is *shown* in place of a broken widget. It does not report anything.

questions.prompt: On first launch, before `fetchAndActivate` has completed, what value does a remote config flag have?
options: The default value set in the app
The last value seen by other users
The call is synchronous: the value is already the remote one
questions.explanation: Fetching is a network call, so on the first run it has not finished. The flag has the default you compiled in — which is why the default must be the safe value, the old behaviour.
whyWrong: It is not null: that is exactly what the defaults are for.
Other people's devices have nothing to do with yours.
It is asynchronous — it is a request over the network.

questions.prompt: What does it take for a Universal Link (iOS) or App Link (Android) to open the app instead of the browser?
options: Just an intent-filter in the manifest
An association file published on the domain plus configuration in the app
Declaring the domain in the store listing
questions.explanation: The point of these links is that they are verified: a file on your domain names your app, and the system checks it. That is what stops anyone else claiming your links — and without it, Android shows the chooser.
whyWrong: A custom scheme is the weak kind: any app can claim it, and in a browser it means nothing.
The intent filter is necessary but not sufficient. Without the published file, no verification happens.
The store listing has no part in link handling.

questions.prompt: A device's push token can change. How do you handle it?
options: Save it once, on first install
Read it again on every launch and listen to `onTokenRefresh`, resyncing the backend
No need to store it: the push service figures it out
Regenerate it yourself every time you send a notification
questions.explanation: The token is the address of that installation, and it changes on reinstall, on restore to a new device, sometimes on an update. Read it at every launch, listen for refreshes, and keep the backend in step — a stale token is a notification delivered to nobody.
whyWrong: Save it once and the first reinstall silently stops that person's notifications for ever.
The service needs a token to deliver to. Keeping your copy current is your job.
You do not generate tokens: the platform does, and tells you when it changes.

questions.prompt: Why does the background push handler have to be top-level and annotated with `@pragma('vm:entry-point')`?
options: It's a style convention of the plugin
Because it's invoked on a fresh isolate and tree shaking must not remove it
Because otherwise it won't compile in debug
questions.explanation: With the app closed, Dart runs the handler in a brand-new isolate with none of your app's state. Nothing in your code calls that function, so tree shaking would delete it; the annotation says "keep this, it is an entry point".
whyWrong: It is not style: without it the function is removed in release and the push silently does nothing.
Functions are not `const`, and that has nothing to do with it.
In debug nothing is tree-shaken, which is exactly why the bug only appears in release.

questions.prompt: What's the most robust setup for an app that has to work offline?
options: Call the network and show an error when it's unavailable
Keep an in-memory cache of the latest responses
Local database as the source of truth, the network updating it, and a queue of pending actions
Lock the UI until the connection comes back
questions.explanation: If the interface reads from the database, it always has something to show. The network only updates the database, and actions taken offline go into a queue — applied locally at once, sent in order when there is signal.
whyWrong: That is the version that is useless on a train: no signal, nothing to show.
Memory is gone when the app is killed, so the next cold start is empty again.
Locking the interface is giving up: the data you already have could be shown.

questions.prompt: Cold start is slow. Where do you begin?
options: Measure with `--trace-startup` and move heavy initialization after the first frame
Switch every SDK to synchronous initialization
questions.explanation: Measure first, because guessing is how you optimise the wrong thing. Then move everything the first frame does not need — analytics, crash reporting, remote config — to after it.
whyWrong: A splash screen hides the wait, it does not shorten it. The numbers stay the same.
Preloading in `main` is the cause of slow startup, not the cure.
Synchronous initialisation blocks the first frame, which makes it worse.

questions.prompt: After a release, crash-free drops from 99.5% to 96%. First move?
options: Immediately prepare a hotfix and upload it to the store
Halt the rollout and remotely switch off the suspect feature
Wait a few days to collect more data
Ask users to reinstall the app
questions.explanation: Stop the bleeding first: pausing the rollout means nobody else gets the broken version, and a flag turns the suspect feature off for those who already have it — both in minutes. The fix comes next, calmly.
whyWrong: A hotfix is right, but it is hours of review plus days of rollout. People keep crashing in the meantime.
You already have the data: a three-point drop right after a release is the signal, not noise.
Reinstalling does not remove the bug, and most people will never see the request.
